title: Design a Search Autocomplete / Typeahead — Trie data structure, top-K suggestions, pre-computed results, caching popular queries, real-time updates.

s1_definition.profdef: A search autocomplete system suggests completions as a user types a prefix, returning the most relevant top-K suggestions with very low latency. The classic structure is a trie that indexes query strings by prefix, with each node storing or pointing to the top-K most popular completions beneath it so results are served in near-constant time. Popular prefixes are precomputed and cached, and the popularity ranking is updated from live query logs.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh starts typing in the National Bank of India app search box — "tra" — the app instantly suggests "transfer money," "transaction history," "track cheque," because those are the most common things customers starting with "tra" want. The app does not scan every possible phrase each keystroke; it keeps a tree of letters where following the path t-r-a lands on a small ready-made list of the best suggestions. That letter tree with ready-made top suggestions is a trie-based typeahead.
s1_definition.oneliner: Index queries in a trie by prefix, precompute top-K popular completions at each node, cache hot prefixes, and refresh rankings from query logs.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A search autocomplete system suggests completions as a user types a prefix, returning the most relevant top-K suggestions with very low latency. The classic structure is a trie that indexes query strings by prefix, with each node storing or pointing to the top-K most popular completions beneath it so results are served in near-constant time. Popular prefixes are precomputed and cached, and the popularity ranking is updated from live query logs.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Rajesh starts typing in the National Bank of India app search box — "tra" — the app instantly suggests "transfer money," "transaction history," "track cheque," because those are the most common things customers starting with "tra" want. The app does not scan every possible phrase each keystroke; it keeps a tree of letters where following the path t-r-a lands on a small ready-made list of the best suggestions. That letter tree with ready-made top suggestions is a trie-based typeahead.

**One line to remember:** Index queries in a trie by prefix, precompute top-K popular completions at each node, cache hot prefixes, and refresh rankings from query logs.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh types in the app search and expects suggestions to appear instantly with each keystroke. If the app searched the entire catalogue of help articles and actions on every letter, it would lag. The real problem is instant prefix lookup over a large vocabulary. This is exactly what a trie with cached top-K completions provides.

Problem 2 — the suggestions must reflect what customers actually search most, so "transfer money" should rank above a rare query, and this ranking must come from real usage. This is exactly how popularity-weighted top-K from query logs works.

Problem 3 — the bank adds a new feature, say "UPI autopay," and wants it to start appearing in suggestions as customers begin searching it, without rebuilding everything on every keystroke. This is exactly how batched real-time ranking updates work.

We build a runnable typeahead core: a `Trie` that inserts queries with frequencies and caches top-K per node, an `AutocompleteService` that serves prefix suggestions and records searches, and a periodic `recomputeTopK`. The demo seeds common banking queries with frequencies, serves suggestions for the prefix "tra," records a surge in a new query, recomputes, and shows the new query rising.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is five seeded banking queries with popularity counts, two prefix lookups, a surge of five hundred searches for a new query, a recompute, and another lookup.

Step 1: Each seeded query is inserted into the trie character by character, and its frequency is stored on the word-ending node. After seeding, `recomputeTopK` walks the trie and fills each node's top-K list with the most popular completions beneath it.

Step 2: The lookup for "tra" walks t, r, a to a node whose cached top-K list holds transfer money, transaction history, and track cheque, sorted by popularity, which is returned instantly.

Step 3: The lookup for "transf" walks further and lands on a deeper node whose top-K holds only completions under that longer prefix, such as transfer money and transfer limit.

Step 4: The new query "transfer to upi" is searched five hundred times via `recordSearch`, raising its frequency. `recomputeTopK` rebuilds the cached lists, so the next lookup for "tra" now includes the surging query in the top three, pushing out the least popular one. The data that changed is the frequency map and the recomputed top-K lists; the trie structure for existing prefixes is unchanged.

```
2026-10-31 23:40:00 [INFO] Suggestions for 'tra': [transfer money, transaction history, track cheque]
2026-10-31 23:40:00 [INFO] Suggestions for 'transf': [transfer money, transfer limit]
2026-10-31 23:40:00 [INFO] recomputed top-K from latest query logs
2026-10-31 23:40:00 [INFO] After surge, 'tra': [transfer money, transaction history, transfer to upi]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  seed queries with frequencies
    │ Trie.insert("transfer money", 1000) ...
    │ recomputeTopK → each node caches top-K
    ▼
  suggest("tra")
    │ walk t → r → a
    │ node.topK (cached) = [transfer money, transaction history, track cheque]
    ▼
  instant suggestions (near O(prefix length))

  recordSearch("transfer to upi") × 500
    │ frequency += 500
    ▼
  recomputeTopK (batched background job)
    │ rebuild node.topK from frequencies
    ▼
  suggest("tra") → now includes "transfer to upi"
```

    Post: returns up to K most popular completions, cached per node

sections.s6_takeaway:
A search autocomplete system suggests completions as the user types a prefix and must return the most relevant top-K suggestions with very low latency. The classic structure I reach for is a trie, a tree where each edge is a character, so walking the path for a prefix lands me on the node representing all queries that start with that prefix. The walk itself costs only as much as the length of the prefix, which is tiny, regardless of how large the vocabulary is.

The key optimization is that scanning every descendant of a prefix node to find the top-K would be too slow for a big vocabulary, so I precompute and cache, at each node, the list of its top-K most popular completions. Answering a prefix query then becomes a prefix walk followed by returning that cached list, which is near-constant time. In the National Bank of India app, typing "tra" instantly returns transfer money, transaction history, and track cheque because those cached lists already hold the most searched completions.

Popularity comes from real query logs, where each search increments a query's frequency, and that frequency drives the ranking of the top-K lists. Because recomputing the whole trie on every keystroke would be far too expensive, I update the rankings in batches: a background job periodically rebuilds the cached top-K lists from recent logs. This is how a newly popular query, like a freshly launched UPI autopay feature, gradually rises into the suggestions as customers search it, without ever slowing down the read path.

The trade-off I always name is between freshness and read speed. Reads have to be instant, so I accept that a brand-new trending query may take a few minutes to appear, which is eventual consistency applied to rankings rather than to data correctness. I also add a cache layer for the hottest prefixes, like single letters, so even the trie walk is skipped, and in a banking context I filter suggestions by the customer's permissions so they never see a completion for an action they cannot perform. That combination of a trie, precomputed top-K, batched ranking updates, and prefix caching is what makes typeahead feel instantaneous even over millions of possible queries.
